from folly. And Saʿīd b. Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: were it not that you give me the lie; and *al-fanadu* is lying, and one says *afnada ifnādan*, he lied, from which
is the poetʾs line: "Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the speech of the truthful any dotage?" — that is, any lie. And it was said: were it not
that you make ugly — said Abū ʿAmr, and *tafnīd* is making ugly, as the poet said: "O my two companions, leave my blaming and my doting, for what has passed of my
affair is not to be returned." And Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: were it not that you weaken my opinion — and Ibn Isḥāq said it; and *al-fanadu* is weakness of opinion from age.
And a fourth saying: you deem me astray — said Abū ʿUbaydah. And al-Akhfash said: you blame me; and *tafnīd* is blaming and weakening of opinion. And al-Ḥasan, Qatādah
and Mujāhid also said: you deem me decrepit; and all of it is close in meaning, and returns to incapacitation and the weakening of opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnīdan*,
when he incapacitated him, as he said: "He destroyed me with blaming and doting"; and one says *afnada*, when he spoke in error, and *al-fanadu* is error in speech and
opinion, as al-Nābighah said, "…guard it from dotage" — that is, prevent it from corruption in the intellect; and from that, blaming is called *tafnīd*, as the poet said:
"O you two who blame me, leave blaming and be brief: the love has been long and you have prolonged the doting." And one says *afnada fulānan al-dahr*, when it corrupted
him, from which is Ibn Muqbilʾs line: "Let the time do what it will, for when it is charged with dotage among men, it dotes." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And when the caravan
departed" from Egypt, "their father said" — Yaʿqūb said to the children who remained with him — "I do indeed feel the smell of Yūsuf, if only you think me not senile,"
except that you might think me senile because of old age. ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said: when the caravan departed from Egypt, a wind started blowing and
brought the scent of Yūsufʾs shirt to Yaʿqūb. He said, "I do indeed feel the smell of Yūsuf, if only you think me not senile." He found his scent from a distance of
eight days away! Similar was also reported through Sufyān al-Thawrī, and Shuʿbah and others reported it from Abū Sinān. "If only you think me not senile": Ibn ʿAbbās,
Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah and Saʿīd b. Jubayr commented, "if only you think me not a fool!" Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said that it means, "if only you think me not old."
**[Jalālayn]** And as the caravan set forth, leaving behind the palm fields of Egypt, their father said to those of his sons and their children present, "Truly I sense
the scent of Joseph" — which the east wind had brought to him with Godʾs permission across a distance of three or eight or more daysʾ journey — "if only you did not
think me doting," if only you did not regard me as foolish, you would believe me. **[Saʿdī]** "And when the caravan set out": from the land of Egypt, coming toward the
land of Palestine; Yaʿqūb smelt the scent of the shirt and said, "I find the scent of Yūsuf, were it not that you would think me doting": that is, were it not that you
would mock me and claim that this speech issued from me without awareness — because he saw from them such marvel at his state as obliged him to say this. **[Study
Quran]** Jacobʾs words were addressed to those of his tribe who were with him. Despite the fact that the caravan was on its way from Egypt to Canaan, Jacob was able to
perceive Josephʾs scent because of the heavenly smell that came from his shirt. Some say that this was a miracle, because Jacob and Joseph were prophets.

**Language.** *Faṣalat al-ʿīr* — *faṣala fuṣūlan* is intransitive and *faṣaltuhu faṣlan* transitive **[Qurṭubī]**. *Ajidu rīḥa* is literally "I find by the sense of
smell" **[Qurṭubī]**. *Lawlā an tufannidūn* is the richest word in the verse and **[Ṭabarī]** gives the definitive analysis: the root of *tafnīd* is corruption
(*ifsād*), so weakness, decrepitude, lying, loss of mind and all meanings of corruption enter into it — corruption in the body being decrepitude, loss of mind and
weakness, and in action being lying and false blaming; therefore all the differing glosses are close in meaning and the apparent sense of the revelation admits all of
them, there being no indicator that one is meant rather than another. The glosses: you deem me foolish (Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah); you deem
me ignorant (Ibn ʿAbbās); his mind has gone (Mujāhid); you give me the lie (Saʿīd, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās); you deem me decrepit (Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan); you
weaken my opinion (Ibn al-Aʿrābī, Ibn Isḥāq); you make ugly (Abū ʿAmr); you deem me astray (Abū ʿUbaydah); you blame me (al-Akhfash). Poetic witnesses: Hāniʾ b.
Shukaym al-ʿAdawī, al-Nābighah, Ibn Muqbil, Jarīr b. ʿAṭiyyah.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** On the distance: eight daysʾ journey (Ibn ʿAbbās via Abū Sinān, and via ʿAbd al-Razzāq at **[Ibn Kathīr]**); eight nights **[Qurṭubī]**; ten nights
(al-Ḥasan); a month (al-Ḥasan); three or eight or more days **[Jalālayn]**. Mālik b. Anasʾs remark is the most striking: the one who brought his scent to him is the
one who brought Bilqīsʾs throne before Sulaymānʾs glance returned to him — i.e. the same order of divine conveyance as 27:40 **[Qurṭubī]**. Mujāhidʾs account makes the
scent that of the Garden itself, spread in the world by the wind striking the shirt **[Qurṭubī]**.

**Belief.** **[Study Quran]** records two explanations and their difference matters: the scent came from the heavenly smell of the shirt; and some say this was a miracle,
because Jacob and Joseph were prophets. The second grounds the perception in prophethood rather than in the object. **[Maʿārif]** will state the doctrine explicitly at
12:94–95: no miracle is in the control of a prophet; a miracle is not even the personal act and action of the prophet — it is directly the act of God; when God wills, He
makes a miracle manifest, and when the divine will is not there, the nearest of the near recedes into the farthest. And **[Ṭabarī]**ʾs concluding judgement — that the
apparent sense admits all the glosses, there being no indicator in the verse — is a model of exegetical restraint on a word about which the Salaf disagreed freely.

**Cross-references.** 12:93 (the shirt sent); 12:95 (the reply); 12:96 (the bearer of good tidings); 12:86 ("I know from God what you do not know"); 27:40 (Bilqīsʾs
throne); 21:69 (the fire made cool); 29:33 and 11:77 ("and when Our messengers came").

**Reflection.** The scent arrives before the news, and it arrives to a blind man. **[Qurṭubī]** is precise about the sense involved: *ajidu* here is finding by smell,
not by sight or by reasoning. So the verse describes a perception that bypasses the organ the narrative has just spent two verses destroying. And the clause that
follows — "were it not that you would think me doting" — is Yaʿqūb pre-empting the exact response he receives at 12:95, which means he knows his household and knows that
a true statement about an unverifiable perception will be received as evidence of senility. **[Saʿdī]** notes the cause: he saw from them such marvel at his state as
obliged him to say it. And **[Ṭabarī]**ʾs treatment of *tafnīd* is itself a lesson in how the tradition handles a word with eleven glosses: rather than choosing, he
shows that all of them share a root — corruption — and that the verse admits all of them. The old man is being told, in eleven ways at once, that his mind has gone; and
he knows it, and says so before they say it.

---

## 12:95

*"They said, ʿBy God, you are in your old error.ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: those who were present with Yaʿqūb of his sons and his sonsʾ sons said to him, when he said "I find the scent of Yūsuf," "By God,
you are in your old error": that is, in your old love of Yūsuf, not forgetting him. *[the reports on this verse are given in the shared block at 12:94]* **[Qurṭubī]**
"They said, by God, you are in your old error": that is, in departure from the path of what is right. And Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd said: in your past mistake, of love for
Yūsuf — you do not forget him. And Saʿīd b. Jubayr said: in your old madness. And al-Ḥasan said: and this is disobedience to parents (*ʿuqūq*). And Qatādah and Sufyān
said: in your old love. And it was said they only said this because Yūsuf, in their view, had died. And it was said that the one who said it to him was those of his sons
who remained with him and did not have the news. And it was said that those of his family and kin who were with him said it. And it was said: his grandchildren, and they
were young — and God knows best. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Their answer to him was, "Certainly, you are in your old error" — meaning, in your old error, according to Ibn ʿAbbās.
Qatādah commented, "They meant that, because of your love for Yūsuf, you will never forget him." So they uttered a harsh word to their father that they should never
have uttered to him, nor to a prophet of God. Similar was said by al-Suddī and others. **[Jalālayn]** They said to him, "By God, you are certainly in your misguidance,"
your error of old, "in your excessive adoration of him and your enduring hope of encountering him again, despite the length of time that has passed." **[Saʿdī]** So what
he suspected of them occurred, and they said, "By God, you are in your old error": that is, you do not cease wandering in a deep sea, not knowing what you say.
**[Maʿārif]** It means that those around Sayyidna Yaʿqūb commented on what he had said by wondering that he still seemed to be engrossed in his old fallacy, that is:
"Yūsuf is alive and we shall meet again." **[Study Quran]** Cf. 12:85–86. By being astray here the brothers mean Jacobʾs overabundant love for Joseph and his hope to
meet with him, which they thought unreasonable under the circumstances as they knew them.

**Language.** *Ḍalāl* here is glossed as departure from the path of what is right **[Qurṭubī]**, past mistake or error (Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd), old madness (Saʿīd b.
Jubayr), old love (Qatādah, Sufyān). The word is not the technical *ḍalāl* of disbelief; it is the ordinary sense of being astray or deluded, which is what makes it
available as a rebuke. **[Saʿdī]** expands it into a metaphor: you do not cease wandering in a deep sea (*baḥr lujjī*), not knowing what you say.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** No reports attach to this verse beyond the glosses; its interest is the identifications of the speakers, which **[Qurṭubī]** gives four ways: those
of his sons who remained with him and did not have the news; those of his family and kin who were with him; his grandchildren, and they were young; or — the reading he
prefers at 12:97 — not his sons at all, because they were absent in Egypt, and the speech would then have been an increase in disobedience to parents.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]**ʾs single word from al-Ḥasan is a ruling: *wa-hādhā ʿuqūq* — and this is disobedience to parents. **[Ibn Kathīr]** says the same more fully:
they uttered a harsh word to their father that they should never have uttered to him, nor to a prophet of God. And **[Qurṭubī]** at 12:97 draws the textual inference that
supports it: in the speech is an elision, the estimation being "so when they returned from Egypt they said, O our father," which indicates that the one who said "by God,
you are in your old error" was his grandchildren or others of his kin and household, not his sons — for they were absent, and it would have been an increase in
disobedience.

**Belief.** **[Study Quran]** supplies the psychology that makes the rebuke intelligible rather than merely cruel: by being astray they meant Jacobʾs overabundant love
and his hope to meet him, *which they thought unreasonable under the circumstances as they knew them*. The circumstances as they knew them were that Yūsuf had been eaten
by a wolf forty years earlier — and **[Qurṭubī]** records that reading: they only said this because Yūsuf, in their view, had died. On that ground the rebuke is not
impiety but a conclusion from evidence. And **[Saʿdī]** notes that Yaʿqūb had anticipated exactly this, which is why he prefaced the statement at 12:94 with "were it not
that you would think me doting": what he suspected of them occurred.

**Cross-references.** 12:94 (the perception); 12:85 ("you will not cease remembering Yūsuf"); 12:86 ("I know from God what you do not know"); 12:96 (the vindication);
12:83 ("it may be that God will bring them all to me"); 23:71 and 5:75 (similar rebukes to prophets).

**Reflection.** The shortest verse in the closing section and the harshest. A man says he smells his son; the people with him say he is mad. The traditionʾs work here is
to decide who "they" were, and **[Qurṭubī]**ʾs reconstruction is the most humane and the most probable: not his sons, who were in Egypt and would return to ask his
forgiveness at 12:97, but his grandchildren or other household — because for his own sons to have said it would have been an increase in disobedience. That reading also
explains the tone: children, hearing an old blind man say he smells a brother who died forty years ago, say what children say. And **[Study Quran]**ʾs note supplies the
rest — they thought his hope unreasonable under the circumstances as they knew them. What they did not know was that the circumstances had changed eight days earlier in
Egypt. The verse therefore records the last moment in the sūrah in which the truth is out of reach of the people present, and it is followed immediately by the verse in
which it arrives.

---

## 12:96

*"And when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it upon his face, and he returned seeing. He said, ʿDid I not say to you that I know from God what you do not know?ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: when the bearer of good tidings came to Yaʿqūb from his son Yūsuf — the one bearing Yūsufʾs message, and that was a courier, as is
related, whom Yūsuf had despatched to him — and the courier and the bearer of good tidings was, as is related, Yahūdhā b. Yaʿqūb, Yūsufʾs brother by his father. Ibn
ʿAbbās said of "when the bearer of good tidings came": the courier. And al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the courier. And Mujāhid said: Yahūdhā b. Yaʿqūb — in four chains. And Ibn
Jurayj said: Yahūdhā b. Yaʿqūb was the bearer of good tidings. And Sufyān said: Ibn Masʿūd used to read, "and the bearer of good tidings came before the caravan." And
al-Suddī said: Yūsuf said, "go with this shirt of mine and cast it upon my fatherʾs face; he will come seeing, and bring me your family all together," and Yahūdhā said,
"I went with the shirt, smeared with blood, to Yaʿqūb and informed him that the wolf had eaten Yūsuf, and I shall go today with the shirt and inform him that he is
alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." So he was the bearer of good tidings. And some of the people of Arabic of Kūfah used to say: the *an* in "when the bearer of
good tidings came" and its omission are of one meaning, and he used to say this of *lammā* and *ḥattā* particularly, and related that the Arabs sometimes bring it in them
and sometimes omit it, as God Most High said "and when Our messengers came" (29:33), and said in another place "and when Our messengers came" (11:77); and he said it is a
connective, with no position in these two places; one says "until it was such-and-such" or "until that it was such-and-such." "He cast it upon his face": the bearer of
good tidings cast Yūsufʾs shirt upon Yaʿqūbʾs face. "And he returned seeing": he returned and came back seeing with his eyes, after he had been blind. "He said, did I
not say to you that I know from God what you do not know": Yaʿqūb said to those of his sons who were present with him at that time: did I not say to you, O my sons, that
I know from God that He will return Yūsuf to me and join me with him, while you did not know of that what I knew — because Yūsufʾs dream was true, and God had decreed
that I and you should prostrate to him, so I was certain of His decree. **[Qurṭubī]** "And when the bearer of good tidings came, he cast it upon his face": that is, upon
his eyes. "And he returned seeing": *an* is extra; and the bearer of good tidings — it was said he was Shimʿūn, and it was said Yahūdhā, who said, "I shall go with the
shirt today as I went with it smeared with blood" — said Ibn ʿAbbās. And from al-Suddī: he said to his brothers, "you know that I went to him with the shirt of grief, so
let me go to him with the shirt of joy." And Yaḥyā b. Yamān said from Sufyān: when the bearer of good tidings came to Yaʿqūb he said to him, "Upon what religion did you
leave Yūsuf?" He said, "Upon Islam." He said, "Now the blessing is complete." And al-Ḥasan said: when the bearer of good tidings came to Yaʿqūb he found nothing with him
to reward him, so he said, "By God, you have found nothing with us, and we have baked nothing for seven nights; but may God make the agonies of death easy for you." I
say: and this supplication is among the greatest of rewards and the best of gifts and stores. And this verse indicates the permissibility of giving and bestowing at good
tidings. And on the subject is the long ḥadīth of Kaʿb b. Mālik, in which: "when the one whose voice I heard giving me good tidings came to me, I took off my two garments
and clothed him with them for his good tidings" — and the ḥadīth is mentioned, and it has preceded in full in the story of the three who were left behind. And Kaʿbʾs
clothing of his two garments to the bearer of good tidings, when he had nothing other than them, is a proof of the permissibility of the like of that when one hopes for
the obtaining of what one rejoices at; and it is a proof of the permissibility of showing joy after the removal of grief and sorrow. And of this chapter is the permissibility
of the boysʾ completion of the Qurʾān, and feeding food on that occasion — and ʿUmar slaughtered a camel after memorising Sūrat al-Baqarah. And God knows best. "He said,
did I not say to you that I know from God what you do not know": he reminded them of his saying, "I complain only of my anguish and my grief to God, and I know from God what
you do not know" (12:86). **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *al-bashīr*, "good news," means information. Mujāhid and al-Suddī said that the bearer of good
news was Yahūdhā, son of Yaʿqūb. Al-Suddī added: he brought Yūsufʾs shirt because it was he who brought Yūsufʾs shirt stained with the false blood; so he liked to erase
that error with this good act, by bringing Yūsufʾs shirt and placing it on his fatherʾs face. His fatherʾs sight was restored to him. Yaʿqūb said to his children, "Did I
not say to you, I know from God that which you know not" — that I know that God will return Yūsuf to me. **[Jalālayn]** Then when — *fa-lammā an*, *an* is extra — the bearer
of good tidings, Judah, came with the shirt — he had been the one who brought the blood-stained shirt, and so now he wished to bring him joy after he had previously brought
him grief — he laid it, he cast the shirt, on his face, and he regained his sight. He said, "Did I not say to you, ʿIndeed I know from God what you do not know?ʾ"
**[Saʿdī]** "And when the bearer of good tidings came": with the nearness of the meeting of Yūsuf and his brothers and their father — "he cast it," that is the shirt, "upon
his face, and he returned seeing": that is, he returned to his former state, seeing, after his eyes had turned white from grief. So he said to those present with him of his
sons and his family, who used to disparage his opinion and marvel at him, triumphing over them and rejoicing in Godʾs blessing upon him: "Did I not say to you that I know
from God what you do not know?" — since I was hoping for the meeting with Yūsuf and awaiting the removal of worry, distress and grief. **[Maʿārif]** Said in verse 96 is
*fa-lammā an jāʾa al-bashīr*: when this man with the good news reached Canaan and put the shirt of Sayyidna Yūsuf over the face of his father, his eyesight returned and he
became a sighted man. The man who came with the good news was Yahūda, the same brother of Sayyidna Yūsuf who had brought his shirt from Egypt. The last sentence of the
verse is: *qāla alam aqul lakum innī aʿlamu min Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn* — that Yūsuf is alive and we shall meet again. **[Study Quran]** Cf. Genesis 45:9–13, 27–28. The
bearer of glad tidings who cast Josephʾs shirt upon Jacobʾs face was the same brother who had earlier interceded with the brothers when they plotted to kill Joseph (see
12:15). For Jacobʾs question, see his announcement in 12:85–86.

**Language.** *Al-bashīr* is glossed by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as *al-barīd*, the courier **[Ṭabarī]**, and by Ibn ʿAbbās as information **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The *an* in
*fa-lammā an jāʾa* is extra **[Qurṭubī] [Jalālayn]**; some of the Kūfan grammarians held its presence and its omission to be of one meaning, and said this of *lammā* and
*ḥattā* particularly, citing 29:33 and 11:77, and classified it as a connective with no grammatical position **[Ṭabarī]**. *Alqāhu ʿalā wajhihi* — upon his face, glossed by
**[Qurṭubī]** as upon his eyes. *Fartadda baṣīran*: *irtadda* means he returned and came back **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Masʿūdʾs reading, "and the bearer of good tidings came
before the caravan," is recorded by Sufyān through **[Ṭabarī]**, who notes in his apparatus that it is not to be read because it contradicts the codex.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Yahūdhāʾs motive is given in three forms: "I went with the shirt smeared with blood to Yaʿqūb and informed him that the wolf had eaten Yūsuf, and I
shall go today with the shirt and inform him that he is alive, and gladden him as I grieved him" (al-Suddī at **[Ṭabarī]**); "I shall go with the shirt today as I went with
it smeared with blood" (Ibn ʿAbbās at **[Qurṭubī]**); "you know that I went to him with the shirt of grief, so let me go to him with the shirt of joy" (al-Suddī at
**[Qurṭubī]**). Sufyānʾs report at **[Qurṭubī]** adds Yaʿqūbʾs first question to the bearer: "Upon what religion did you leave Yūsuf?" — "Upon Islam." — "Now the blessing is
complete." And al-Ḥasanʾs report of the reward: Yaʿqūb had nothing to give him and had baked nothing for seven nights, so he prayed, "may God make the agonies of death easy
for you" — of which **[Qurṭubī]** says, this supplication is among the greatest of rewards and the best of gifts and stores. The ḥadīth of Kaʿb b. Mālik is cited in full:
"when the one whose voice I heard giving me good tidings came to me, I took off my two garments and clothed him with them for his good tidings" — and Kaʿbʾs giving of his two
garments when he had nothing other than them is the proof.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]**: this verse indicates the permissibility of giving and bestowing at good tidings (*jawāz al-badhl wa-l-hibāt ʿinda al-bashāʾir*), established by
the ḥadīth of Kaʿb b. Mālik; and it indicates the permissibility of showing joy after the removal of grief and sorrow; and of this chapter is the permissibility of celebrating
the boysʾ completion of the Qurʾān and feeding food on that occasion — ʿUmar slaughtered a camel after memorising Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Maʿārif]** makes the same two points:
the giving of a reward to someone who brings good news is a practice of the blessed prophets, as in the well-known event of Kaʿb b. Mālik, who gave the dress he was wearing to
the man who brought him news that his repentance had been accepted.

**Belief.** Yaʿqūbʾs question is a vindication and **[Ṭabarī]** gives its ground precisely: I know from God that He will return Yūsuf to me and join me with him, *because
Yūsufʾs dream was true and God had decreed that I and you should prostrate to him, so I was certain of His decree*. The knowledge he claimed at 12:86 was therefore not
intuition but certainty about a decree, and 12:96 is the moment that certainty becomes visible. **[Saʿdī]** adds the affective clause: he said it to those who used to
disparage his opinion and marvel at him, *triumphing over them and rejoicing in Godʾs blessing upon him* — a rare instance of the exegete allowing a prophet a moment of
vindication.

**Cross-references.** 12:15 (the well, and the brother who interceded); 12:18 (the false blood); 12:84 (the eyes turning white); 12:86 ("I know from God what you do not
know"); 12:93 (the shirt sent); 12:97 (the request for forgiveness); 12:100 (the prostration); 29:33; 11:77; the ḥadīth of Kaʿb b. Mālik (Bukhārī, Muslim); Genesis
45:9–13, 27–28 **[Study Quran]**.

**Reflection.** The verse reverses two objects at once: the eyes that whitened from weeping are restored, and the shirt that carried a lie now carries a cure. And the man
who carries it is chosen for the symmetry — **[Study Quran]** identifies him as the brother who had interceded when they plotted to kill Joseph, and **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**
and **[Ibn Kathīr]** all preserve his own reason: I grieved him with this shirt, so let me gladden him with it. Yaʿqūbʾs first question to him, in Sufyānʾs report, is not
"where is my son?" but "upon what religion did you leave Yūsuf?" — and the answer, "upon Islam," produces "now the blessing is complete." That single exchange states the
scale on which the prophets measure recovery. And the closing question — "did I not say to you that I know from God what you do not know?" — is directed, **[Ṭabarī]**
specifies, at those of his sons who were present, the ones who had just called him senile. He does not gloat; he reminds them of a sentence they heard at 12:86 and did not
believe.

---

## 12:97

*"They said, ʿO our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; we were indeed sinners.ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: the sons of Yaʿqūb who had separated him from Yūsuf said, "O our father, ask our Lord to pardon us and cover our sins, which we sinned
against you and against Yūsuf, so that He not punish us for them on the Day of Resurrection; we were indeed sinners in what we did to him, and we have acknowledged our sins."
*[the section continues into 12:98]* **[Qurṭubī]** "They said, O our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; we were indeed sinners": in the speech is an elision, the
estimation being: so when they returned from Egypt they said, O our father. And this indicates that the one who said to him, "by God, you are in your old error," was his
grandchildren or others of his kin and household, not his sons, for they were absent — and it would have been an increase in disobedience. And God knows best. And they only
asked him for forgiveness because they had brought upon him of the pain of grief what the offence was not dropped from except by his releasing them. I say: and this ruling is
established for whoever harmss a Muslim in his person or his wealth or otherwise, wronging him — it is incumbent upon him to seek release from him and inform him of the
grievance and its extent. And does an unqualified release benefit him or not? There is disagreement, and the correct view is that it does not benefit him, because if he
informed him of a grievance of weight and consequence, perhaps the soul of the wronged would not be content to release it. And God knows best. And in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī
and others, from Abū Hurayrah: the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Whoever has a grievance against his brother, of his honour or anything, let him seek release from him today,
before there is no dinar and no dirham; if he has righteous work, it will be taken from him in the measure of his grievance, and if he has no good deeds, the sins of his
companion will be taken and carried upon him." Al-Muhallab said: his saying ﷺ "it will be taken from him in the measure of his grievance" requires that the grievance be of
known extent, pointed to and specified; and God knows best. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is when Yūsufʾs brothers said to their father, with humbleness, "O our father! Ask forgiveness
from God for our sins, indeed we have been sinners." **[Jalālayn]** They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; truly we have been sinful." **[Saʿdī]** So they
acknowledged their sin, and benefited by that, and said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us of our sins; we were indeed sinners": in that we did with you what we did.
**[Maʿārif]** Now, when the truth of the matter became clear, the brothers of Yūsuf asked for the forgiveness of their father in a spiritually endearing style by saying, "Our
father, pray to God to forgive us our sins. Surely we have been wrong." Thus it is obvious that a person who prays to God for the forgiveness of their sins would do that
himself too. **[Study Quran]** This conversation occurred after the brothers returned home from Egypt. Some record that Jacob delayed his prayer for forgiveness a certain
period of time, perhaps to ascertain whether they were being sincere and truthful.

**Language.** *Istaghfir lanā dhunūbanā*: *istaghfara* is to ask forgiveness, and **[Ṭabarī]** unpacks it as "ask our Lord to pardon us and cover our sins" — the two senses
of *ghafara*, pardon and concealment. *Khāṭiʾīn* is from *khaṭiʾa*, to commit an offence deliberately, as at 12:91; **[Saʿdī]** specifies the object: in that we did with you
what we did. The elision in the verse — that they said this *after returning from Egypt* — is **[Qurṭubī]**ʾs contribution and it settles who had spoken at 12:95.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** draws from the verse the sūrahʾs clearest legal principle on the rights of persons: they only asked him for forgiveness because they had brought
upon him of the pain of grief what the offence was not dropped from except by his releasing them (*illā bi-iḥlālihi*). And this ruling is established for whoever harms a Muslim
in his person or his wealth or otherwise, wronging him: it is incumbent upon him to seek release from him and to inform him of the grievance and its extent. Does an
unqualified release benefit him? There is disagreement, and the correct view is that it does not, because if he informed him of a grievance of weight, perhaps the soul of the
wronged would not be content to release it. The ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah is given in full, and al-Muhallabʾs inference from "in the measure of his grievance" is that the
grievance must be of known extent, pointed to and specified. **[Maʿārif]** makes the complementary point: unless the victim of injustice forgives, there is no forgiveness from
God either; no violation of the rights of the servants of God is forgiven unless the holder of the right receives his right back or forgives it — verbal repentance alone is not
enough. And he adds an observation about the request itself: it is obvious that a person who prays to God for the forgiveness of their sins would do that himself too.

**Belief.** **[Study Quran]** records the reason for the delay at 12:98 that is most often given: perhaps to ascertain whether they were being sincere and truthful. That
reading makes the delay a test rather than a liturgical preference, and it is compatible with the other explanations preserved at **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** — the last third
of the night, the eve of Friday, the white nights, or (al-Shaʿbī) that Yaʿqūb would first ask Yūsuf whether he had pardoned them.

**Cross-references.** 12:91 (the confession to Yūsuf); 12:92 (Yūsufʾs pardon, the *iḥlāl*); 12:96 (the sight restored); 12:98 (the deferred supplication); 12:18 (the first
deception of the father); the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah on grievances (Bukhārī); 24:22; 42:40.

**Reflection.** The confession is addressed to the father, not to God, and the reason is legal rather than sentimental. **[Qurṭubī]** is explicit: they asked him because
they had brought upon him a pain of grief that would not be dropped except by his release. Yūsuf had already pardoned them at 12:92, so what remained was the second creditor,
and **[Maʿārif]**ʾs principle explains why Yaʿqūbʾs supplication could not simply be pronounced over them: without the release, the sin against the person is not forgiven,
and a supplication for what has not been released would be premature. That is why Yaʿqūb answers at 12:98 with *sawfa*, "I shall" — a future tense, not a present one. And
**[Qurṭubī]**ʾs inference about the elision resolves a difficulty the reader has been carrying since 12:94: the ones who called him senile were not these men, who were in Egypt,
but the grandchildren or other household. So the sūrah ends by separating two groups — those who mocked his hope and those who now ask his forgiveness — and puts the request in
the mouths of the second.

---


## 12:98

*"He said, ʿI shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: Yaʿqūb said, "I shall ask my Lord to pardon your sins, which you sinned against me and against Yūsuf." Then the people of knowledge differed about the time to which Yaʿqūb deferred the supplication for his sons, seeking forgiveness for them of their sin. Some said: he deferred it to the last part of the night before dawn. And ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd said: Yaʿqūb deferred his sons to the *saḥar* by his saying "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." And Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said: he deferred them to the *saḥar*. And ʿAmr b. Qays said: in the prayer of the night. And Ibn Jurayj said: he deferred that to the *saḥar*. And others said: he deferred it to the night of Friday — from ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās from the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord": he says, until the night of Friday comes. **[Qurṭubī]** "He said, I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord": Ibn ʿAbbās said, he deferred his supplication to the *saḥar*. And al-Muthannā b. al-Ṣabbāḥ said from Ṭāwūs: the *saḥar* of the night of Friday, and that coincided with the night of ʿĀshūrāʾ. And in the supplication of preservation — from the book of al-Tirmidhī — from Ibn ʿAbbās: while we were with the Messenger of God ﷺ, ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib came to him and said, "May my father and mother be your ransom — this Qurʾān has slipped from my chest, and I find that I am unable to hold it." So the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him, "Shall I not teach you words by which God will benefit you and benefit whoever you teach, and establish what you have learned in your chest?" He said, "Yes, O Messenger of God — so teach me." He said, "When it is the night of Friday, then if you are able to stand in the last third of the night, for it is a witnessed hour and supplication in it is answered — and my brother Yaʿqūb said to his sons, *I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord*, saying: until the night of Friday comes." And he mentioned the ḥadīth. And Ayyūb b. Abī Tamīmah al-Sikhtiyānī said from Saʿīd b. Jubayr: "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord" — in the white nights, the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth, for supplication in them is answered. And from ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī: "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord" — that is, I shall ask Yūsuf; if he pardons you, I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. And Sunayd b. Dāwūd said: Hushaym related to us, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Isḥāq related to us, from Muḥārib b. Dithār, from his uncle: I used to come to the mosque at the *saḥar* and pass by the house of Ibn Masʿūd and hear him saying, "O God, You commanded me and I obeyed, and You called me and I answered, and this is the *saḥar*, so forgive me." So I met Ibn Masʿūd and said, "Words I hear you saying at the *saḥar*." He said, "Yaʿqūb deferred his sons to the *saḥar* by his saying, ʿI shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lordʾ." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "He said: I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you, verily, He! Only He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful," and He forgives those who repent to Him. ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, ʿAmr b. Qays, Ibn Jurayj and several others said that the prophet Yaʿqūb delayed fulfilling their request until the latter part of the night. **[Jalālayn]** He said, "Assuredly I shall ask forgiveness for you of my Lord. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful" — he, Jacob, put off this plea of forgiveness until the last hour before dawn, in order to be closer to the likelihood of it being accepted, or he put it off until the eve of Friday. They then departed for Egypt, where Joseph and the senior courtiers came out to meet them. **[Saʿdī]** So he said, answering their request and hastening to answer them: "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; He is the Forgiving, the Merciful": and my hope in Him is that He forgive you and have mercy on you and envelop you in His mercy. And it has been said that he deferred the seeking of forgiveness for them to the excellent time of the *saḥar*, so that it would be more complete in seeking forgiveness and nearer to being answered. **[Maʿārif]** The reply given by Sayyidna Yaʿqūb was: "I shall pray to my Lord to forgive you." Here Sayyidna Yaʿqūb has, instead of praying for them instantly, made a promise that he would pray for them soon. Commentators have generally given a reason for this: according to them, his purpose was to pray for them particularly, in peace and with concentration, towards the later part of the night — because the prayer made at that hour is answered specially. This is as it appears in a ḥadīth in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī and Muslim that, in the last third part of every night, God descends in all His glory close to the firmament near the earth, and proclaims: "Is there someone who would pray to Me, and I would answer? Is there someone who would seek forgiveness from Me, and I would forgive?" **[Study Quran]** Some record that Jacob delayed his prayer for forgiveness a certain period of time, perhaps to ascertain whether they were being sincere and truthful.

**Language.** *Sawfa astaghfiru lakum rabbī*: *sawfa* marks the future and, unlike *sa*, carries a sense of deferral; the verse is the standard proof-text in Arabic rhetoric for *taswīf*, postponement in a promise. *Al-saḥar* is the last part of the night before dawn; *al-layālī al-bīḍ* are the white nights, the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of the lunar month **[Qurṭubī]**. *Innahu huwa al-ghafūru al-raḥīm* is given by **[Ṭabarī]** as the ground of the promise, and by **[Ibn Kathīr]** with the addition: and He forgives those who repent to Him.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Five explanations of the deferral are preserved: (1) to the *saḥar* — Ibn Masʿūd (two chains at **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]**), Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, ʿAmr b. Qays ("in the prayer of the night"), Ibn Jurayj, Ibn ʿAbbās; (2) to the night of Friday — from ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās *from the Messenger of God ﷺ*, and the long ḥadīth of ʿAlī in al-Tirmidhīʾs book of supplications, in which the Prophet ﷺ teaches him the words for retaining the Qurʾān and cites Yaʿqūbʾs deferral to the night of Friday as precedent; (3) Ṭāwūs: the *saḥar* of the night of Friday, coinciding with the night of ʿĀshūrāʾ; (4) Saʿīd b. Jubayr via Ayyūb: the white nights, because supplication in them is answered; (5) al-Shaʿbī: I shall ask Yūsuf — if he pardons you, I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. The ḥadīth of the divine descent in the last third of the night (Bukhārī, Muslim) is cited by **[Maʿārif]** as the ground of the whole preference.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]**ʾs first numbered ruling, drawn jointly from 12:97–98, is the *ḥuqūq al-ʿibād* principle stated at 12:97: no violation of the rights of the servants of God is forgiven unless the holder of the right receives his right back or forgives it. And one of the reasons commentators give for the delay is that Yaʿqūb first wanted to check with Yūsuf whether or not he had forgiven them, because unless the victim of injustice forgives, there is no forgiveness from God either — so, this being the state of affairs, making a prayer for forgiveness was not appropriate. Al-Shaʿbīʾs reading at **[Qurṭubī]** is the same point read as the plain sense of the verse. **[Maʿārif]** also cites the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah in Bukhārī: a person who has someoneʾs financial right due against him, or who has caused pain by word or action, must pay it back today or get it off his shoulders by seeking forgiveness — before the Day of Resurrection, when no one will have property or wealth from which rights could be paid; so his good deeds will be given to the victim and he will be left empty-handed, and if he has no good deeds, the sins of the other person will be put on his shoulders.

**Belief.** The deferral is read three ways and each implies something different about Yaʿqūb. The liturgical reading — the *saḥar*, the night of Friday, the white nights — makes the delay an act of precision: he is choosing the hour in which supplication is answered, which is what **[Maʿārif]** gives with the descent ḥadīth and **[Saʿdī]** with "more complete in seeking forgiveness and nearer to being answered." The juridical reading — al-Shaʿbīʾs "I shall ask Yūsuf" — makes it an act of order: the human creditor must release before the divine forgiveness can be sought. **[Study Quran]**ʾs reading, through al-Rāzī, makes it an act of prudence: perhaps to ascertain whether they were being sincere and truthful. **[Saʿdī]** also notes the affective reading, which is the plainest: he said it *answering their request and hastening to answer them* — so the deferral is in the grammar but not in the intention.

**Cross-references.** 12:97 (the request); 12:92 (Yūsufʾs pardon); 12:99–100 (the arrival); 12:86 ("I know from God what you do not know"); 2:156; 39:53; 40:60; 51:18 ("and in the last part of the night they sought forgiveness"); 3:17; the descent ḥadīth (Bukhārī, Muslim); the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah on grievances (Bukhārī); the ḥadīth of ʿAlī in al-Tirmidhī.

**Reflection.** Yaʿqūb has just been vindicated — his sight returned, his sons confessing — and the first thing he does with the vindication is promise a supplication rather than make one. The tradition has spent more commentary on the word *sawfa* than on the rest of the verse, because the deferral is the whole content. Five explanations, four of them about timing and one about justice. The timing explanations are not trivia: Ibn Masʿūdʾs habit of saying at the *saḥar*, "You commanded me and I obeyed, and You called me and I answered, and this is the *saḥar*, so forgive me," is a practice built on this verse, and the Prophetʾs ﷺ instruction to ʿAlī cites Yaʿqūbʾs deferral to the night of Friday as the precedent for a supplication meant to hold the Qurʾān in the chest. The juridical explanation, al-Shaʿbīʾs, is the more searching: I shall ask Yūsuf; if he pardons you, I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. On that reading Yaʿqūb will not pray for a debt that has not been released — which is why Yūsufʾs "no reproach upon you today" at 12:92 had to come first, and why **[Maʿārif]** can say that making the prayer was not appropriate until it had. And **[Saʿdī]** keeps the two together: he answered their request, hastening to answer them, and chose the hour in which the answer would be heard.

---


## 12:99

*"And when they entered upon Yūsuf, he gave his parents lodging with himself, and said, ʿEnter Egypt, if God wills, in safety.ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: when Yaʿqūb and his sons and their families entered upon Yūsuf, he gave his parents lodging with himself, and said to them, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety." And if someone says: how did Yūsuf say to them, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety," after they had entered it, when God has informed of them that when they entered upon Yūsuf and he drew his parents to himself, he said this to them? — it is said: the interpreters differed about that. Some said: Yaʿqūb only entered upon Yūsuf, he and his sons, and Yūsuf drew his parents to himself before entering Egypt; and that was because Yūsuf went out to meet his father in honour of him before he entered Egypt, and drew him to himself, then said to him and to those with him, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety," before the entering. And al-Suddī said: they carried to him their families and their dependants, and when they reached Egypt, Yūsuf spoke to the king who was above him, and he went out, and the kings went out to meet them; and when they reached Egypt he said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety" — "and when they entered upon Yūsuf, he gave his parents lodging with himself." And Farqad al-Sabakhī said: when the shirt was cast upon his face he returned seeing, and said, "bring me your family all together"; so Yaʿqūb and Yūsufʾs brothers set out, and when he drew near, Yūsuf was informed that he had drawn near him, so he went out to meet him; and the people of Egypt rode with him, for they used to magnify him. And when the two drew near to one another — and Yaʿqūb was walking, leaning on a man of his sons called Yahūdhā — Yaʿqūb looked at the horses and the people and said, "O Yahūdhā, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said, "No — this is your son!" And when each of the two drew near to the other, Yūsuf went to begin him with the greeting, and was prevented from that, for Yaʿqūb was more entitled to it than he and more excellent; so Yaʿqūb said, "Peace be upon you, O you who take away my griefs." And it reached me that Yūsuf and the king went out with four thousand to meet Yaʿqūb and his sons. *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]* And others said: rather His words "if God wills" are an exception from Yaʿqūbʾs saying to his sons, "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"; and it is of the deferred whose meaning is brought forward. They said: the meaning of the speech is, he said: I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord, if God wills; He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. And when they entered upon Yūsuf he gave his parents lodging with himself, and said, "Enter Egypt," and he raised his parents. **[Qurṭubī]** "And when they entered upon Yūsuf": that is, upon a palace he had there. "He gave his parents lodging with himself": it was said that Yūsuf sent with the bearer of good tidings two hundred riding-camels and equipment, and asked Yaʿqūb to come to him with his family and his sons all together; and when they entered upon him he drew his parents to himself, that is, embraced them — and he means by his two parents his father and his maternal aunt, and his mother had died at the birth of his brother Binyāmīn. And it was said that God revived his mother for him in verification of the dream, so that she prostrated to him — said al-Ḥasan; and it has preceded in Sūrat al-Baqarah that God Most High revived for His Prophet ﷺ his father and his mother, and they believed in him. "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety": Ibn Jurayj said, that is, "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord, if God wills" — he said, and this is of the Qurʾānʾs bringing forward and deferring. Al-Naḥḥās said: Ibn Jurayj goes to the view that they had already entered Egypt, so how does he say, "Enter Egypt, if God wills"? And it was said that he only said "if God wills" for blessing and certainty. "In safety": from dearth, or from Pharaoh, and they used not to enter it except with his passage. *[the section continues into 12:100]* **[Ibn Kathīr]** God states that Yaʿqūb went to Yūsuf in Egypt. Yūsuf had asked his brothers to bring all of their family, and they all departed their area and left Canaan for Egypt. When Yūsuf received news of their approach to Egypt, he went out to receive them. The king ordered the princes and notable people to go out in the receiving party with Yūsuf to meet Godʾs prophet Yaʿqūb. It is said that the king also went out with them to meet Yaʿqūb. Yūsuf said to his family, after they entered unto him and he took them to himself, "and said: Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security." He said to them, enter Egypt, meaning reside in Egypt, and added, if God wills, in security, in reference to the hardship and famine that they suffered. God said next, "and he took his parents to himself": al-Suddī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Zayd b. Aslam said that his parents were his father and maternal aunt, as his mother had died long ago. Muḥammad b. Isḥāq and Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī said, "His father and mother were both alive." Ibn Jarīr added, "There is no evidence that his mother had died before then. Rather, the apparent words of the Qurʾān testify that she was alive." This opinion has the apparent and suitable meaning that this story testifies to. **[Jalālayn]** And when they entered to Joseph in his tent, he took his parents — his father and his mother, or and his maternal aunt — into his arms and said, "Enter into Egypt, if God will, in safety." And they entered, and Joseph sat down on his throne. **[Saʿdī]** That is, when Yaʿqūb and his sons and their families had all equipped themselves and set out from their land, intending to arrive at Yūsuf in Egypt and to dwell in it, and when they arrived at him and entered upon Yūsuf, he gave his parents lodging with himself: that is, he drew them to himself, singled them out with his nearness, and showed them of kindness, goodness, reverence and magnification something immense. And he said to all his family: "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in safety": from all disliked things and fears. So they entered in this gladdening state, and toil was removed from them and the misery of life, and joy and gladness were obtained. **[Maʿārif]** It appears in some narrations that Sayyidna Yūsuf had sent with his brothers this time a large supply of clothes and other articles of need, all loaded on some two hundred camels, so that the whole family could make good preparations in anticipation of their visit to Egypt. Thus, all set for the trip, when Sayyidna Yaʿqūb and his entire family set out for Egypt, their number, according to one narration, was seventy-two and, according to another, it was comprised of ninety-three men and women. On the other side, when came the time for their arrival in Egypt, Sayyidna Yūsuf and the people of Egypt came out of the city to receive them. With them came four thousand soldiers to present a guard of honour. When these guests reached Egypt and entered the home of Sayyidna Yūsuf, he lodged his parents with him. Here the text refers to "parents," though the mother of Sayyidna Yūsuf had died during his childhood; but after her death Sayyidna Yaʿqūb had married Layyā, the sister of his late wife. She was, in her capacity as the maternal aunt of Sayyidna Yūsuf, almost like his own mother, and also as the married wife of his father, deserving of being called nothing but his mother. This interpretation is according to the report which says that the mother of Sayyidna Yūsuf had died at the time of Benyāmīnʾs birth. On this basis the present text of the respected author appears to be contradictory to the relevant text on page 38 of Volume V, where the name of Sayyidna Yūsufʾs mother has been given as Rāḥīl. But in reality there is no authentic report in this connection; Isrāʾīlī reports do exist, but they too are contradictory. The author of *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* has himself said that the Jewish chroniclers do not subscribe to the view that the mother of Sayyidna Yūsuf had died at the time of Benyāmīnʾs birth. If this report is given credence, no doubt remains; then in this situation, by the words "and he raised his parents up on the throne" (12:100), the reference would be to the real mother of Sayyidna Yūsuf. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Kathīr have opted for this as the weightier view; so, commenting on this, Ibn Kathīr has said: Ibn Jarīr said, no evidence has been established for the death of his mother, and the apparent sense of the Qurʾān indicates that she was alive. At the end of verse 99, the statement "he said, Enter Egypt, God willing, in peace" means that Sayyidna Yūsuf asked all his family members to enter Egypt by the will of God and without any fear or restriction, the sense being that they were free from the usual restrictions placed on travellers who enter another country. *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]* **[Study Quran]** For "enter … in security, if God wills" with reference to the Prophet Muḥammad and his followers, see 48:27, which states that the Muslims shall enter the Sacred Mosque in security, if God wills.

**Language.** *Āwā ilayhi abawayhi*: *āwā* means he drew to himself and gave lodging to, as at 12:69; *abawayhi* is the dual of parent and is the point of dispute. *Udkhulū Miṣra in shāʾa Llāhu āminīn* — *āminīn* is glossed by **[Qurṭubī]** as safe from dearth or from Pharaoh, since they used not to enter Egypt except with his passage, and by **[Maʿārif]** as free from the usual restrictions placed on travellers entering another country. The position of *in shāʾa Llāh* is the grammatical problem: either it belongs with "enter Egypt" (the majority), or it is an exception from Yaʿqūbʾs "I shall ask forgiveness for you from my Lord," on the principle of the Qurʾānʾs bringing forward and deferring (Ibn Jurayj, via **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]**). Al-Naḥḥās answers Ibn Jurayj: he goes to the view that they had already entered Egypt, so how does he say "enter Egypt, if God wills"? And it was said he only said "if God wills" for blessing and certainty.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The meeting scene is elaborated at **[Ṭabarī]**: Yūsuf goes out to meet his father in honour of him before entering Egypt; the people of Egypt ride with him because they magnified him; Yaʿqūb walks leaning on Yahūdhā; seeing the horses and the people he asks, "is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" and is told, "no — this is your son"; and when Yūsuf goes to greet him first, he is prevented, because Yaʿqūb was more entitled to it and more excellent, so Yaʿqūb says, "Peace be upon you, O you who take away my griefs." And it reached me that Yūsuf and the king went out with four thousand to meet Yaʿqūb and his sons. *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]* **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same with the king ordering the princes and notables into the receiving party, and **[Maʿārif]** adds the four thousand soldiers as a guard of honour and the two hundred camels of clothes and supplies sent ahead. On the parents: al-Suddī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Zayd held the mother was the maternal aunt, the mother having died long ago; Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Jarīr held both were alive, with Ibn Jarīr adding that there is no evidence the mother had died and the apparent words of the Qurʾān testify she was alive — the view **[Ibn Kathīr]** prefers and **[Maʿārif]** adopts after weighing the contradictory Isrāʾīlī reports. Al-Ḥasanʾs alternative — that God revived his mother for him in verification of the dream, so that she prostrated — is recorded at **[Qurṭubī]**, who compares it to the report that God revived the Prophetʾs ﷺ own father and mother and they believed in him.

**Belief.** The dispute about the mother is not antiquarian: it determines whether the prostration at 12:100 fulfils the dream literally, since the dream had the sun and the moon among the eleven stars. If the mother was dead, either the maternal aunt stands in her place, or God revived her so that the dream could be verified — al-Ḥasanʾs solution, which **[Qurṭubī]** records without endorsing. **[Study Quran]**ʾs note is the one that connects the verse to the Islamic present: "enter in security, if God wills" is the same formula as 48:27, where the Muslims are promised entry to the Sacred Mosque in security, if God wills — so the familyʾs arrival in Egypt and the communityʾs arrival at Makkah share a phrase.

**Cross-references.** 12:4–6 (the dream); 12:93 (the shirt and "bring me your family"); 12:96 (the sight restored); 12:98 (the deferred supplication); 12:100 (the prostration and the throne); 12:67 (the gates of Egypt); 48:27 ("you shall enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security").

**Reflection.** The verse is the sūrahʾs arrival, and the tradition cannot resist enlarging it. **[Ṭabarī]**ʾs report gives the detail that matters most: Yūsuf went to greet his father first and *was prevented from that*, because Yaʿqūb was more entitled to it and more excellent — so the father says the greeting, and says it in words that summarise forty years, "peace be upon you, O you who take away my griefs." That single exchange reverses 12:84: the man who cried "O my grief for Yūsuf" now addresses the one who removes it. And Yaʿqūbʾs question on the road — "is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" — is the last moment of non-recognition in the sūrah, answered with "no, this is your son." The grammatical difficulty about *in shāʾa Llāh* is worth noticing because it is generated by the narrativeʾs own compression: they had already entered when he said "enter," which is why Ibn Jurayj transferred the exception to 12:98. The simpler answers are better — that it is said for blessing and certainty, or, as **[Maʿārif]** has it, that Yūsuf was granting them entry free of the restrictions placed on travellers. And the dispute about the mother is the sūrahʾs last unresolved question, left honestly unresolved by **[Maʿārif]**: there is no authentic report, Isrāʾīlī reports exist, and they contradict one another.

---


## 12:100

*"And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell prostrate before him. And he said, ʿO my father, this is the interpretation of my dream of old; my Lord has made it true. And He has been good to me when He brought me out of the prison and brought you from the desert, after Satan incited between me and my brothers. My Lord is subtle in what He wills; He is the Knower, the Wise.ʾ"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God says: he raised his parents upon the throne — and the throne here is the seat of the kingdom. "And they fell prostrate before him": Yaʿqūb, his wife and his sons prostrated before Yūsuf, and the prostration was a greeting and not a worship; and that was their greeting among themselves, the low to the high, and it was permitted in their law and abrogated in our law. "And he said, O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream of old": this is the outcome of my dream which I saw when I said to you, "I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me," and this is its verification. "My Lord has made it true": He has made it a true thing and not confused dreams. "And He has been good to me when He brought me out of the prison": God has been good to me in His bringing me out of the prison in which I was confined, and in His bringing you from the desert. And Yaʿqūbʾs dwelling and his sonsʾ was, as is related, in the desert of Palestine; so Ibn Isḥāq said: the dwelling of Yaʿqūb and his sons was, as some of the people of knowledge mentioned to me, at al-ʿArabāt in the land of Palestine, the marches of Syria — and some say at al-Awlāj in the region of al-Shaʿb, and he was a man of the desert, with camels and sheep; and Qatādah said of "and He brought you from the desert": Yaʿqūb and his sons were in the land of Canaan, people of livestock and wilderness; and Ibn Jurayj said: they were people of the desert and livestock. And *al-badw* is a verbal noun from the saying of one who says "so-and-so went to the desert" (*badā fulān*), when he came to be in the desert, *yabdū badwan*. And it is related that Yaʿqūb entered Egypt, he and those with him of his sons, their families and their children, on the day they entered it, being fewer than a hundred; and they went out of it on the day they went out being more than six hundred thousand. And ʿAbdullāh b. Shaddād said: the family of Yaʿqūb gathered to Yūsuf in Egypt, and they were eighty-six persons, their young and their old, their male and their female; and they went out of Egypt on the day Pharaoh brought them out, and they were six hundred thousand and more. And from Ibn Masʿūd: the Banū Isrāʾīl entered Egypt as sixty-three persons and went out of it as six hundred thousand — and Isrāʾīl said, six hundred thousand and seventy thousand. And Masrūq said: the family of Yūsuf entered Egypt as three hundred and ninety, between man and woman. "After Satan incited between me and my brothers": after he corrupted what was between me and them, and some of us was ignorant toward some. One says *nazagha al-shayṭānu bayna fulān wa-fulān, yanzaghu nazghan wa-nuzūghan*. "My Lord is subtle in what He wills": my Lord is possessed of subtlety and making for what He wills; and of His subtlety and making is that He brought me out of the prison, and brought my family from the desert, after what was between me and them of distance of abode, and after what I was in of servitude, slavery and captivity. And Qatādah said of "my Lord is subtle in what He wills": He was subtle with Yūsuf and made for him, until He brought him out of the prison, and brought his family from the desert, and removed from his heart the incitement of Satan and his stirring up against his brothers. "He is the Knower": of the interests of His creation and other than that; nothing of the beginnings of matters and their outcomes is hidden from Him. "The Wise": in His arrangement. And al-Ḥasan said: Yūsuf was cast into the well at seventeen years of age, and he was in servitude and in prison and in kingship eighty years; then God gathered his kin, and he lived after that twenty-three years; so he died at a hundred and twenty. And in another report from al-Ḥasan: he was absent from his father eighty years, and Yaʿqūbʾs eyes did not dry, and there was no one upon the earth more noble with God than Yaʿqūb. And Ibn Isḥāq said: it was mentioned to me, and God knows best, that Yūsufʾs absence from Yaʿqūb was eighteen years; and the People of the Book claim it was forty years or thereabouts, and that Yaʿqūb remained with Yūsuf after he came to him in Egypt seventeen years, then God took him. *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]* **[Qurṭubī]** "And he raised his parents upon the throne": Qatādah said, he means the bed; and its senses have preceded — the throne may be used of the kingdom and of the king himself, from which is al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānīʾs line: "thrones — they perished after might and security." "And they fell prostrate before him": in it are three *masāʾil*. **The first**: the *hāʾ* in "they fell prostrate before him" — it was said that it returns to God Most High, the meaning being: they fell prostrating in gratitude to God, and Yūsuf was like the direction of prayer, in verification of his dream; and it is related from al-Ḥasan. Al-Naqqāsh said: and this is an error; the *hāʾ* returns to Yūsuf, because of His words at the beginning of the sūrah, "I saw them prostrating to me." And their greeting was that the low prostrated to the high and the young to the old; and Yaʿqūb, his maternal aunt and his brothers prostrated to Yūsuf, and his skin crept and he said, "This is the interpretation of my dream of old." And between Yūsufʾs dream and its interpretation were twenty-two years; and Salmān al-Fārisī and ʿAbdullāh b. Shaddād said, forty years; and ʿAbdullāh b. Shaddād said: and that is the furthest a dream is delayed. And Qatādah said, thirty-five years; and al-Suddī, Saʿīd b. Jubayr and ʿIkrimah said, thirty-six; and al-Ḥasan, Jisr b. Farqad and Fuḍayl b. ʿIyāḍ said, eighty years. And Wahb b. Munabbih said: Yūsuf was cast into the well at seventeen years of age, and was absent from his father eighty years, and lived after meeting his father twenty-three years, and died at a hundred and twenty — and in the Torah, a hundred and twenty-six. And Efrāthīm and Manassā, and Raḥmah the wife of Ayyūb, were born to Yūsuf from the wife of the ʿAzīz. And between Yūsuf and Mūsā were four hundred years. And it was said that Yaʿqūb remained with Yūsuf twenty years, then died; and it was said he stayed with him eighteen years; and some of the traditionists said, twenty-four; and between Yaʿqūb and Yūsuf were thirty-three years until God gathered them. And Ibn Isḥāq said, eighteen years — and God knows best. **The second**: Saʿīd b. Jubayr said from Qatādah from al-Ḥasan concerning "and they fell prostrate before him": it was not a prostration, but a custom they had, in which they nodded with their heads, and that was their greeting. And al-Thawrī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said: it was a prostration like the prostration known to us, and that was their greeting. And it was said it was a bowing like the *rukūʿ*, and was not a falling to the ground; and so was their greeting, by inclining and bowing. And God abrogated all of that in our law and made speech in place of bowing. And the interpreters agreed that that prostration, in whatever form it was, was only a greeting and not a worship; Qatādah said: this was the greeting of kings among them, and God gave this community the *salām*, the greeting of the people of the Garden. I say: this bowing and inclining that was abrogated from us has become a custom in the lands of Egypt and among the Persians, and likewise their standing up for one another, until one of them, if he is not stood up for, feels in himself as though no regard is paid to him and he has no worth; and likewise when they meet, some bow to others, a continuing custom and an established inheritance, especially at the meeting of the commanders and the chiefs. They have turned away from the sunnah. And Anas b. Mālik related: we said, "O Messenger of God, does one of us bow to his companion when we meet?" He said, "No." We said, "Does one of us embrace another?" He said, "No." We said, "Does one of us shake hands with another?" He said, "Yes." — recorded by Abū ʿUmar in *al-Tamhīd*. And if it is said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Stand up for your lord and your best," meaning Saʿd b. Muʿādh — we say: that was specific to Saʿd, because of what the particular situation required; and it has been said that their standing was only to bring him down from the donkey. And also: it is permitted for the older man if it does not affect his soul; but if it affects him and he is pleased by it and sees a share for himself in it, it is not permitted to help him to that, because of his saying ﷺ, "Whoever is pleased that people stand up for him, let him take his seat in the Fire." And it came from the Companions that there was no face more noble to them than the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they did not stand up for him when they saw him, because of what they knew of his dislike of that. **The third *masʾalah***: if it is said, what do you say about pointing with the finger? — it is said to him: that is permitted when he is far from you, so that you designate the time of the greeting for him by it; but if he is near, then no. And it has been said that it is forbidden in both nearness and distance, because of what came from the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever resembles other than us is not of us," and "Do not greet with the greeting of the Jews and the Christians, for the greeting of the Jews is with the palms and of the Christians with pointing." And when he greets, he does not bow, nor kiss his hand along with the greeting, because bowing in the sense of humility is not fitting except for God. As for kissing the hand, it is of the practice of the non-Arabs, and they are not to be followed in the practices they invented out of magnification of their chiefs, because the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not stand at my head as the non-Arabs stand at the heads of their kings." And there is no harm in shaking hands, for the Prophet ﷺ shook hands with Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib when he came from Abyssinia, and commanded it and urged it, and said, "Shake hands — resentment will go." And Ghālib al-Tammār related from al-Shaʿbī that the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, when they met, shook hands, and when they came from a journey, embraced. And if it is said: Mālik disliked shaking hands — we say: Ibn Wahb related from Mālik that he disliked shaking hands and embracing, and Saḥnūn and others of our companions went to this; and the contrary is related from Mālik, that shaking hands is permitted, and that is what the meaning of what is in the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* indicates, and a group of scholars of the Salaf and the Khalaf hold the permissibility of shaking hands. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Mālik only disliked shaking hands because he did not see it as a general matter in the religion, nor transmitted as the *salām* is transmitted; and had it been of the sunnah he would have held it equal. I say: a ḥadīth has come concerning shaking hands indicating the encouragement to it, diligence in it and constancy in it, which is what al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib related: I met the Messenger of God ﷺ and he took my two hands, and I said, "O Messenger of God, I used to think shaking hands was for the non-Arabs!" He said, "We are more entitled to shaking hands than they are. No two Muslims meet and one takes his companionʾs hand out of affection between them and sincerity, but their sins are shed between them." "And he has been good to me when He brought me out of the prison," and did not say "from the well," out of the use of generosity, so as not to remind his brothers of their act after his pardon of them by his saying "no reproach upon you." I say: and this is the root with the shaykhs of the Sūfis — mentioning estrangement at the time of intimacy is estrangement — and it is a sound saying indicated by the Book. And it was said: because his entering the prison was by his own choice, by his saying "my Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they call me to" (12:33), whereas his being in the well was by Godʾs will for him. And it was said: because he was in the prison with thieves and sinners, and in the well with God Most High; and also the favour in deliverance from the prison was greater, because he entered it by reason of their affair, and also entered it by his own choice. And Yaʿqūb said: praise be to God, who gladdened my eyes after worries and griefs — and he entered Egypt with eighty-two of his household, and they did not leave Egypt until they were more than six hundred thousand and some; and they crossed the sea with Mūsā — related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās. And Ibn Masʿūd related that they entered Egypt as ninety-three persons, between man and woman, and went out with Mūsā as six hundred and seventy thousand. And al-Rabīʿ b. Khaytham said: they entered it as seventy-two thousand and went out with Mūsā as six hundred thousand. And Wahb said: Yaʿqūb and his sons entered Egypt as ninety persons, between man, woman and child, and went out of it with Mūsā fleeing from Pharaoh as six hundred thousand five hundred and some seventy fighting men, apart from the offspring, the aged and the infirm — and the offspring were twelve hundred thousand, apart from the fighters. And the people of histories said: Yaʿqūb dwelt in Egypt twenty-four years in the most enviable state and blessing, and died in Egypt, and charged his son Yūsuf to carry his body and bury it with his father Isḥāq in Syria; so he did, then returned to Egypt. Saʿīd b. Jubayr said: Yaʿqūb was carried in a coffin of teak to Jerusalem, and that coincided with the day ʿĪṣū died, so they were buried in one grave; and from that the Jews carry their dead to Jerusalem, whoever of them does that. And Yaʿqūb and ʿĪṣū were born in one belly and buried in one grave, and their age together was a hundred and forty-seven years. *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And he raised his parents to al-ʿArsh": he raised them to his bedstead where he sat, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and several others. God said, "and they fell down before him prostrate": Yūsufʾs parents and brothers prostrated before him, and they were eleven men. "And he said: O my father! This is the interpretation of my dream aforetime," in reference to the dream that he narrated to his father before, "I saw eleven stars" (12:4). In the laws of these and previous prophets, it was allowed for the people to prostrate before the men of authority when they met them. This practice was allowed in the law of Ādam until the law of ʿĪsā, but was later prohibited in our law. Islam made prostration exclusively for God alone, the Exalted and Most Honoured. The implication of this statement was collected from Qatādah and other scholars. When Muʿādh b. Jabal visited the Levant, he found them prostrating before their priests. When he returned to Madīnah, he prostrated before the Messenger of God ﷺ, who asked, "What is this, O Muʿādh?" Muʿādh said, "I saw that they prostrate before their priests. However, you, O Messenger of God, deserve more to be prostrated before." The Messenger ﷺ said, "If I were to order anyone to prostrate before anyone else among the creation, I would have ordered the wife to prostrate before her husband because of the enormity of his right on her." Therefore, this practice was allowed in previous laws, as we stated. This is why Yaʿqūb, his wife and eleven sons prostrated before Yūsuf, who said at that time, "O my father! This is the interpretation of my dream aforetime! My Lord has made it come true!" — using the word *taʾwīl* to describe what became of the matter later on. God said in another verse, "Await they just for its *taʾwīl*? On the Day the event is finally fulfilled" (7:53), meaning, on the Day of Judgement what they were promised of good or evil will surely come to them. Yūsuf said, "My Lord has made it come true!" — mentioning that God blessed him by making his dream come true — "and He was indeed good to me, when He took me out of the prison, and brought you all here out of the bedouin life," out of the desert, for they lived a bedouin life and raised cattle, according to Ibn Jurayj and others. He also said that they used to live in the ʿAravah, Ghūr area of Palestine, in Greater Syria. Yūsuf said next, "after Satan had sown enmity between me and my brothers. Certainly, my Lord is the Most Courteous and Kind unto whom He wills" — for when God wills something, He brings forth its reasons and elements of existence, then wills it into existence and makes it easy to attain. "Truly, He! Only He is the All-Knowing," of what benefits His servants, "the All-Wise," in His statements, actions, decrees, preordainment and what He chooses and wills. **[Jalālayn]** And he raised his parents, he seated them next to him upon the throne, and they fell down, that is, his parents and brothers, prostrating before him — a prostration that was actually a bowing down, not placing their foreheads down on the ground; this was their standard form of greeting at that time. Then he said, "O father, this is the interpretation of my vision of old. Indeed my Lord has made it true. And indeed He has been gracious to me since He brought me out of the prison" — he did not say "out of the well," in a show of magnanimity, lest his brothers feel ashamed — "and has brought you from the desert, after Satan had incited ill feeling, made trouble, between me and my brethren. Truly my Lord is Subtle in bringing about what He will. Truly He is the Knower of His creatures, the Wise in His actions." His father Jacob remained with him for twenty-four years, or for seventeen years. The duration of his separation from Joseph had been eighteen, or forty, or eighty years. When death approached him he charged Joseph to take him and bury him by his father Isaac; and so he, Joseph, himself went and buried him there. He, Joseph, then returned to Egypt and remained alive for another twenty-three years. **[Saʿdī]** "And he raised his parents upon the throne": that is, upon the bed of the kingdom and the seat of the ʿAzīz. "And they fell prostrate before him": that is, his father, his mother and his brothers, a prostration of magnification, veneration and honour. "And he said," when he saw this state and saw their prostration to him: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream of old": when he saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon prostrating to him — so this is its occurrence, to which it came and at which it arrived. "My Lord has made it true": He did not make it confused dreams. "And He has been good to me": with an immense goodness, "when He brought me out of the prison and brought you from the desert" — and this is of His gentleness and the goodness of his speech; for he mentioned his state in the prison and did not mention his state in the well, out of the completeness of his pardon from his brothers, and that he would not mention that sin; and that your coming from the desert is of Godʾs goodness to me — so he did not say, "He brought you from hunger and toil," and did not say, "He was good to you," but said, "He was good to me," making the goodness return to himself. So blessed be He who singles out with His mercy whom He wills of His servants and bestows upon them mercy from Himself; He is the Bestower. "After Satan incited between me and my brothers": and he did not say, "Satan incited my brothers"; rather, it was as though the sin and the ignorance issued from both sides. So praise be to God, who shamed Satan and drove him away and gathered us after that grievous separation. "My Lord is subtle in what He wills": He brings His kindness and goodness to the servant from where he does not perceive, and brings him to high stations through matters he dislikes. "He is the Knower": who knows the outward of matters and their inward, and the secrets of the servants and what is in their breasts. "The Wise": in His placing things in their places and His driving matters to their appointed times. **[Maʿārif]** Verse 100 opens with the words "and he raised his parents up on the throne": Sayyidna Yūsuf had his parents sit with him on the royal throne. After that it was said, "and they all fell before him in prostration": the parents, and all brothers, did prostration before Sayyidna Yūsuf. Sayyidna ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAbbās has said that this prostration of gratitude was for God, and not for Sayyidna Yūsuf. Others have said that prostration as part of worship, when done for anyone other than God, has always been forbidden in the *sharīʿah* of every prophet; but the prostration of veneration (*taʿẓīm*) was permissible in the religious codes of past prophets — which has been prohibited in the *sharīʿah* of Islam on the basis that it is a source of *shirk*. This is confirmed by ḥadīth reports from al-Bukhārī and Muslim that prostration for anyone other than God is not lawful. And when both his father and mother, and eleven of his brothers, prostrated before him simultaneously, he remembered the dream he had seen in his childhood, and he said: "My father, here is the fulfilment of my early dream," that the sun and the moon and eleven stars are prostrating to me, and I am grateful that "my Lord has made it come true." **Rules and points of guidance**: (1) When his sons requested Yaʿqūb to pray for their forgiveness, he said, "I shall soon pray to my Lord to forgive you" — he did not make that supplication instantly; he delayed it. One of the reasons given by commentators for this delay is that he first wanted to check with Yūsuf whether or not he had forgiven them, because unless the victim of injustice forgives, there is no forgiveness from God either; so this being the state of affairs, the making of a prayer for forgiveness was not appropriate. Pointed to here is a matter of sound principle: no violation of the rights of the servants of God is forgiven unless the holder of the right receives his right back or forgives it — verbal repentance for it is not enough. (2) According to a narration of Sufyān al-Thawrī, when Yahūda brought in the shirt of Sayyidna Yūsuf and put it over the face of his father, he asked, "How is Yūsuf?" Yahūda told him that he was the king of Egypt. Sayyidna Yaʿqūb said, "I am not asking if he is a prince or a pauper; I am asking how he is in his faith and deed." Then he told him about the qualities of his character and how God-fearing and chaste in conduct he was. This is how the noble prophets love and relate to their children: they are more concerned about the state of their spiritual life than with the state of their physical comfort. This is the model every Muslim should follow.
