(3) According to Ḥasan, when the carrier of the good news arrived with the shirt of his separated son, Yaʿqūb wished to give him something in reward; but life was hard, therefore he apologised that there was no bread baked in the house for seven days and he could not give a material reward — however, he prayed that God make the agony of death easy on him. Al-Qurṭubī has said that this prayer was the best reward for him. (4) This event also tells us that the giving of a reward to someone who brings good news is a practice of the blessed prophets; the event relating to Kaʿb b. Mālik is well known. In addition, it also proves that inviting friends over meals on occasions of happiness is sunnah: ʿUmar, when he completed his reading of Sūrat al-Baqarah, shared his happiness with others by inviting them to eat with him, for which he slaughtered a camel. (5) The sons of Yaʿqūb, once the truth had come out in the open, asked for the forgiveness of their father and brother. This tells us that a person who has caused pain to someone by word or action, or remains responsible for returning any right owed to him, must pay back that right immediately or have it forgiven by him — per the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah in Bukhārī. **Patience and gratitude: the dignified station of Sayyidna Yūsuf.** To pick up the thread of the story, Sayyidna Yūsuf starts telling his parents things which happened to him. This is a point where it would be useful to stop for a while and think. Had someone in our day been subjected to all those hardships which were faced by Sayyidna Yūsuf, and had he been enabled to meet his parents after such a long trial of separation and disappointment, just imagine where he would begin his tale of woes, how he would cry and make others do the same, and how many days and nights he would spend recounting the hardships faced by him. But the two parties, the teller and the listener, are both no less than two messengers and prophets of God. Worth observing is their conduct in this matter. Here is the very dear separated son of Sayyidna Yaʿqūb, when he meets his father after having gone through the long period of so many hardships — see what he says: "He favoured me when He released me from the prison and brought you from the countryside after Satan had caused a rift between me and my brothers." The hardships faced by Sayyidna Yūsuf can be divided over three stages: (1) the injustices of his brothers; (2) the separation from his parents; (3) the pain of the prison. What this great prophet of God has done is that, in his statement, he has changed the order of events as they had happened. He started from the prison. Then he said nothing about how he had entered the prison and how he had suffered there; rather, he talked about how he was released from the prison, and mentioned that too with words of gratitude for God. As a corollary of his release from the prison and his gratitude to God for it, he also told them that he had been in the prison for a certain time. Worth noticing here is that Sayyidna Yūsuf has mentioned his release from the prison, but he has not said anything about the prison of the well in which his brothers had thrown him. He did not mention it even functionally, as in "He released me from the prison." The reason is that he had already forgiven the mistake made by his brothers, and had said, "No reproach upon you today" (12:92). Therefore he did not consider it proper to mention the incident of the well in any form whatsoever, so that his brothers might not be put to shame (Qurṭubī). After that, he was supposed to dwell on the long and trying separation from his parents, and talk about how they had affected him. But he set all these things aside. He took up the last part of it and mentioned his meeting with the parents, and said so by thanking God for it: "and brought you from the countryside" to this city of Egypt. There is a hint here to the blessing of God, that He brought Sayyidna Yaʿqūb from his home in the countryside, where conveniences of living are scarce, to a city with royal honours. The first stage of the trials of Sayyidna Yūsuf has not been mentioned yet. This concerns the injustices inflicted by his brothers on him. It is interesting that he sweeps the whole thing away as a handiwork of Satan, and makes things come easy even by suggesting that his brothers were not of the kind who would do something like that: it was Satan who deceived them and caused this rift between them. This is the elegance of prophets: not only that they would be patient against pain and hardship, but that they would invariably find the occasion to be grateful to God under all conditions. Therefore, with prophets, there is no state of being in which they are not grateful to God. This is contrary to what ordinary human beings do: in their state of being, thousands of blessings of God would be showered over them, yet they would not talk about them to anyone; and when some hardship overtakes them at some time, they would go about crying over it all their lives. The Qurʾān has complained about this human mind-set when it says, "human beings are, to their Lord, very ungrateful" (100:6). After having reduced the tale of his trials in three words, Sayyidna Yūsuf said: "Surely, my Lord does what He wills in a subtle way. Surely, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise." **[Study Quran]** Joseph raised his parents up to the throne; that is, he seated them upon the kingʾs throne. For Josephʾs vision of which this verse is the fulfilment, see 12:4. "They all" refers to Josephʾs parents and his eleven brothers, which correspond to the sun, the moon, and the eleven stars, respectively. Prostrating toward someone was a way of greeting and honouring that person, much like standing up for someone out of respect or kissing the hand. Joseph does not mention the well from which he was delivered, only the prison, since he had already told his brothers in 12:92, "there is no reproach against you this day." Josephʾs blaming Satan for having incited evil between himself and his brothers is tantamount to his making an excuse for them for their wrong actions (see also 12:89–90). Josephʾs description of God as "Subtle in that which He wills" means that the manner in which God carries out His Will is subtle (cf. Genesis 46:5–7).

**Language.** *Al-ʿarsh* is the bed or seat of the kingdom, and may be used of the kingdom and of the king himself, per al-Nābighahʾs "thrones — they perished after might and security" **[Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]**. *Kharrū lahu sujjadan*: *kharrū* means they fell, and *sujjadan* a prostration — glossed by **[Jalālayn]** as a bowing down, not placing the foreheads on the ground, which was their standard form of greeting at that time; by al-Ḥasan as not a prostration but a custom of nodding with the head **[Qurṭubī]**; by al-Thawrī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as a prostration like the prostration known to us, which was their greeting; and by others as a bowing like the *rukūʿ*, their greeting being by inclining and bowing. *Nazagha al-shayṭānu baynī wa-bayna ikhwatī*: *nazagha … yanzaghu nazghan wa-nuzūghan*, to corrupt between two parties, here glossed as "he corrupted what was between me and them, and some of us was ignorant toward some" **[Ṭabarī]**; **[Saʿdī]** notes that he did not say "Satan incited my brothers," but as though the sin and the ignorance issued from both sides. *Al-badw* is a verbal noun from *badā fulān yabdū badwan*, to come to be in the desert **[Ṭabarī]**; **[Ibn Kathīr]** locates it in the ʿAravah, Ghūr area of Palestine, in Greater Syria. *Laṭīf* is glossed by **[Ṭabarī]** as possessed of subtlety and making for what He wills; by **[Saʿdī]** as bringing His kindness and goodness to the servant from where he does not perceive, and bringing him to high stations through matters he dislikes; by **[Ibn Kathīr]** as bringing forth the reasons and elements of existence for what He wills, then willing it into being and making it easy to attain. *Taʾwīl* is used here, as at 7:53, to describe what became of the matter later on **[Ibn Kathīr]**.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]**ʾs three *masāʾil* on *kharrū lahu sujjadan* are the standard legal treatment of prostration to other than God. (1) The *hāʾ* returns to Yūsuf, not to God — al-Naqqāsh calls the contrary reading of al-Ḥasan an error — and their greeting was the prostration of the low to the high, which was permitted in their law and abrogated in ours; the interpreters agreed that the prostration, in whatever form, was only a greeting and not a worship, and Qatādah said this was the greeting of kings among them, while God gave this community the *salām*, the greeting of the people of the Garden. (2) The bowing and inclining abrogated from us has become a custom in Egypt and among the Persians, as has standing up for one another, until one who is not stood up for feels he has no worth — and they have turned away from the sunnah; the ḥadīth of Anas: "does one of us bow to his companion when we meet?" — "No"; "does one embrace another?" — "No"; "does one shake hands?" — "Yes"; and "stand up for your lord and your best" was specific to Saʿd b. Muʿādh, or their standing was to bring him down from the donkey; standing is permitted for the older man if it does not affect his soul, but if it does and he sees a share for himself, it is not permitted to help him to that, per "whoever is pleased that people stand up for him, let him take his seat in the Fire." (3) Pointing with the finger is permitted at a distance to designate the time of the greeting, but not near — and it has been said to be forbidden in both cases, per "whoever resembles other than us is not of us" and "do not greet with the greeting of the Jews and the Christians"; and he does not bow or kiss his hand along with the greeting, because bowing in the sense of humility is not fitting except for God, and kissing the hand is of the practice of the non-Arabs, per "do not stand at my head as the non-Arabs stand at the heads of their kings." Shaking hands is not harmful: the Prophet ﷺ shook hands with Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib when he came from Abyssinia, and said "shake hands — resentment will go"; al-Shaʿbī: the Companions shook hands when they met and embraced when they came from a journey; Mālik disliked it because he did not see it as a general matter in the religion nor transmitted as the *salām* is — but the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib indicates encouragement of it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ruling historically: in the laws of these and previous prophets it was allowed for people to prostrate before men of authority when they met them; this was allowed from the law of Ādam until the law of ʿĪsā, and was later prohibited in our law, Islam making prostration exclusively for God; with the ḥadīth of Muʿādh b. Jabal in full. **[Maʿārif]** states the same with the added ground: prostration as part of worship for other than God has always been forbidden in the *sharīʿah* of every prophet, but the prostration of veneration was permissible in the codes of past prophets and has been prohibited in Islam *on the basis that it is a source of shirk*, confirmed by ḥadīth reports from Bukhārī and Muslim.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** Muʿādh b. Jabal in the Levant, his prostration to the Prophet ﷺ, and the answer: "if I were to order anyone to prostrate before anyone else among the creation, I would have ordered the wife to prostrate before her husband because of the enormity of his right on her" **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Anasʾs three questions — bowing, embracing, shaking hands — and the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ: "no two Muslims meet and one takes his companionʾs hand out of affection between them and sincerity, but their sins are shed between them" **[Qurṭubī]**. "Whoever is pleased that people stand up for him, let him take his seat in the Fire"; "whoever resembles other than us is not of us"; "do not greet with the greeting of the Jews and the Christians"; "do not stand at my head as the non-Arabs stand at the heads of their kings"; "shake hands — resentment will go" **[Qurṭubī]**. The Companions not standing for the Prophet ﷺ because of what they knew of his dislike **[Qurṭubī]**. Sufyān al-Thawrīʾs report of Yaʿqūbʾs first question to Yahūdhā — "how is Yūsuf?" — and his correction, "I am not asking if he is a prince or a pauper; I am asking how he is in his faith and deed" **[Maʿārif]**. The chronologies: between the dream and its interpretation, twenty-two years, forty (Salmān al-Fārisī, ʿAbdullāh b. Shaddād, who adds "and that is the furthest a dream is delayed"), thirty-five (Qatādah), thirty-six (al-Suddī, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrimah), eighty (al-Ḥasan, Jisr b. Farqad, Fuḍayl b. ʿIyāḍ), eighteen (Ibn Isḥāq), thirty-three **[Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]**. Yūsufʾs age: cast into the well at seventeen, absent eighty years, lived twenty-three after the meeting, died at a hundred and twenty — and in the Torah, a hundred and twenty-six (Wahb b. Munabbih) **[Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]**. Efrāthīm, Manassā and Raḥmah the wife of Ayyūb born to Yūsuf from the wife of the ʿAzīz; four hundred years between Yūsuf and Mūsā **[Qurṭubī]**. The numbers entering Egypt: eighty-six (ʿAbdullāh b. Shaddād), sixty-three (Ibn Masʿūd), three hundred and ninety (Masrūq), eighty-two (Ibn ʿAbbās via ʿIkrimah), ninety-three (Ibn Masʿūd via **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Maʿārif]**), seventy-two thousand (al-Rabīʿ b. Khaytham), ninety (Wahb); and leaving: more than six hundred thousand, six hundred and seventy thousand, six hundred thousand five hundred and some seventy fighting men apart from twelve hundred thousand offspring **[Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]**. Yaʿqūb dwelt in Egypt twenty-four years in the most enviable state, died there, and charged Yūsuf to carry his body and bury it with Isḥāq in Syria; Saʿīd b. Jubayr: he was carried in a teak coffin to Jerusalem, coinciding with the day ʿĪṣū died, so they were buried in one grave — and from that the Jews carry their dead to Jerusalem; Yaʿqūb and ʿĪṣū were born in one belly and buried in one grave, and their age together was a hundred and forty-seven years *[Isrāʾīliyyāt]*.

**Belief.** Three doctrines close the sūrah. First, the abrogation: the prostration was a greeting permitted in their law and abrogated in ours, and **[Maʿārif]** gives the ground — it is a source of *shirk*. Second, the excuse for the brothers: Yūsuf attributes the whole affair to Satan, and **[Study Quran]**, through al-Qushayrī, calls this tantamount to making an excuse for them for their wrong actions; **[Saʿdī]** notes the grammar of that generosity — he did not say "Satan incited my brothers," but as though the sin and the ignorance issued from both sides. Third, divine subtlety: *inna rabbī laṭīfun limā yashāʾ*, glossed by **[Saʿdī]** as bringing His kindness to the servant from where he does not perceive and bringing him to high stations through matters he dislikes — which is the sūrahʾs whole plot in one clause, since the well, the slave-market, the solicitation and the prison were all matters Yūsuf disliked and all stages of the ascent. **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the general account: when God wills something, He brings forth its reasons and elements of existence, then wills it into being and makes it easy to attain. And **[Maʿārif]**ʾs meditation on the ordering of Yūsufʾs speech is the traditionʾs final word on prophetic conduct: he changed the order of events as they had happened, began with the prison and its release, said nothing of how he entered it or suffered in it, did not mention the well even functionally, set aside the long separation from his parents and mentioned only the meeting with them as a blessing, and swept away the injustices of his brothers as a handiwork of Satan. This is the elegance of prophets — not only patience against hardship but an invariable occasion for gratitude; whereas ordinary human beings, showered with thousands of blessings, do not speak of them, and when one hardship overtakes them, cry over it all their lives, of which the Qurʾān complains: "human beings are, to their Lord, very ungrateful" (100:6).

**Cross-references.** 12:4 (the dream, now interpreted); 12:6 and 12:21 (*taʾwīl*); 12:15 (the well); 12:23–29 (the solicitation); 12:33 ("prison is more beloved to me"); 12:36–41 (the prison); 12:54–56 (the establishment); 12:67–68 (the gates and the precaution); 12:84 (the whitened eyes); 12:86 ("I know from God what you do not know"); 12:92 ("no reproach upon you today"); 12:93 (the shirt); 12:99 (the entry); 7:53 ("await they but its *taʾwīl*"); 48:27; 6:83 ("We raise in degrees"); 40:15; 100:6; 2:124 (Ibrāhīm an imam); Genesis 46:5–7 **[Study Quran]**.

**Reflection.** The sūrahʾs narrative closes not with the reunion but with an interpretation. "O my father, this is the *taʾwīl* of my dream of old" — the word used at 12:6 and 12:21 of the meaning that arrives after the event, applied here to a boyʾs vision decades before. And the second half of the verse is a summary of the whole narrative delivered in a form that omits most of it. **[Maʿārif]**ʾs analysis is the sharpest thing said about this verse in any of the seven sources: Yūsuf changed the order of events as they had happened; he began with the prison and its release; he said nothing about the well, not even functionally, because he had already pardoned them and did not want to shame them; he passed over the long separation and mentioned only the meeting, as a blessing; and he attributed the brothersʾ injustice to Satan, in a construction — "between me and my brothers" — that shares the fault. **[Qurṭubī]** names the principle behind the omission in a phrase that became proverbial among the Sūfis: mentioning estrangement at the time of intimacy is estrangement. And **[Saʿdī]** catches the smallest and most characteristic detail: he said "He has been good to *me*," not "He has been good to you," making the goodness return to himself — so that even the familyʾs deliverance from famine is counted as a favour to the one who was thrown into a well. The closing names describe the method: subtle in what He wills, bringing the servant to high stations through matters he dislikes; the Knower, who knows the outward and the inward; the Wise, who places things in their places and drives matters to their appointed times. That is the sūrahʾs answer to itself. The well, the slave-market, the prison, the famine, the cup in the saddlebag — each was a matter Yūsuf disliked, and each was a stage of the ascent; and the man who saw eleven stars prostrating to him at the beginning is the man who, at the end, will not mention the well.

---
